title: Tournament Analysis
text: So far we’ve looked at trends for broad categories, such as GI vs NO-GI or Female vs Male, but when we get more granular do our conclusions continue to hold? Perhaps at Brazilian Nationals we’ll see the Weight you need to be to podium tends to be higher due to Brazil being the most developed region. Maybe for Euros we’ll see a lower weight doing well, given Europe tends to have a thinner population compared to somewhere like the U.S. Or perhaps well see a clear divide between Euros and Brazilian Nationals compared to Pans and Worlds. As arguably Worlds and Pans are higher tiered tournaments.

title: Placing Analysis
text:
This page seeks to see if there are underlying trends based one what placing a competitor took in both the Absolute class and their own weight class.


When we look at each individual placing, 1 through 3, in the absolute and compare it to the weight weight class of the competitor a few insights appear.

We see the general trend of Medium Heavy to Super Heavy being the weight classes that perform the best that we saw in our overview still holds even at the individual placing level.
More intrestingly we see taking 2nd and 3rd in the absolute have very similair breakdowns of weight classes, but for taking 1st we see a much higher proportion of competitors fall in the Heavy and particularly the Super Heavy classes, with the Medium Heavy weight class having a significant drop off. The Super Heavy and Heavy weight classes by themselves make up 50% of the 1st place winners.














When looking at the relationship between how well a competitor placed in their weight class in comparison to the Absolute class, unsurprisingly we see that the better a competitor does in their weight class the more likely they are to do well in the absolute class. Although it is still striking to see that nearly %80 of 1st place winners of the absolute took 1st int their weight class. In short taking 1st in your weight class is a very strong signal you will perform well in the absolute.









When we look at the overall distribution of Competitors that made the podium in the absolute class, we see the trend of 1st place winners from the weight class performing well in the absolute holds. Out of all competitors who placed in the absolute at all the vast majority were those who had placed 1st in their weight class division.

title: Introduction
text:
Brazilian Jiu Jitsu, BJJ for short, is often said to be a sport suited for smaller individuals. Allowing smaller individuals the ability to defeat larger opponents through a combination of technique, timing, and leverage. Flipping the common notion that size and strength are the primary deciding factors in who wins a fights on its head. This idea is often used to promote BJJ as a sport and self defense system and is commonly talked about in the BJJ community. As an avid practitioner and competitor of the sport for many years I’ve often been the skeptical person in conversations around “does size matter”. My experience has been that while BJJ does allow a smaller opponent to beat a larger one that this largely only applies when the larger opponent is untrained in combat sports and the size discrepancy is not to large.
In BJJ competition there is a division called the Absolute Class where the idea that “size doesn’t matter” is on full display. The Absolute Class is a division where competitors compete against each other regardless of their weightclass. For example a 127.0lb Rooster weight competitor can compete against a 222.0lb Super Heavy competitor in an Absolute Class bracket. So, if BJJ does allow a smaller opponent to beat a larger one we should see smaller competitors winning the absolute class in tournaments. While we see this at smaller local level tournaments does this still hold true at the highest level of competition? Where the competitors are all extremely skilled and equally dedicated to the sport.
In this project I’m combining my passion for BJJ with my professional data analysis skills to see what does the data really say. In the hopes of answering the question, how much do you really need to weigh to win or place in the Absolute Division at a Major BJJ tournament.
For the project I’m looking at tournament results from the IBJFF. The oldest, largest, and arguably most prestigious tournament organizer in Jiu Jitsu. I’m only looking at what I consider to be the four major IBJJF tournaments:
-IBJJF Worlds
-IBJJF Pans
-IBJFF Europeans
-IBJJF Brazilian Nationals
*Note: Brazilian Nationals is included as a major tournament, because with the sport originating in Brazil it was long thought that Brazilian Nationals was as or more difficult to win as the other 3 major tournaments. Due to the fact that the sport was more developed in the Brazil with many of the best athletes living and comepting there but unable to travel to the other 3 tournaments for primariily financial reasons.

My Jiu Jitsu Journey:
As of Jan 2026 I’ve been training BJJ for a little over five years. I started training in Colorado Springs, Co before moving to Chicago, IL as a blue belt. In my first four years I was a very active competitor, competing several times a year, traveling all over the USA, and having done 20+ competitions. I plan to begin competing more regularly again in 2026.
In the last two years I’ve began teaching at my gym when our main instructors are unable to teach due to travel, sickness, etc… I’ve found I have a true passion for teaching and hope to continue to get more opportunities to do so in the future.
While, I’ve always trained and competed in both Gi and No-Gi I have a special passion for the Gi with my favorite technique being the berimbolo.
Jiu Jitsu came into my life during a time where I was dealing with very difficult personal issues. At the time it gave me something positive to focus on and put my energy into. I’m very grateful for what the sport and the community has done for me.

title: BJJ Absolute Class Analysis
text:
This project aims to determine using data what weight a competitor needs to be to have realistic chance of winning the Absolute class at the highest levels.
The project looks at Tournament data from the entire history of the IBJJF. Only considering the Black Belt level for both GI and No-GI at the following major tournaments.
IBJJF Worlds
IBJJF Pans
IBJJF Europeans
Brazilian Nationals

First Look
On our first look of the data a few insights stand out.

There is clear up tick in placings starting at Medium Heavy and a consistent drop off at Ultra Heavy. This leads me to believe that you need to be big enough to place in the absolute, but weight has diminishing returns. We likely see the drop off at Ultra Heavy due to many of these athletes being Ultra Heady due to excess body weight and not necessarily pure size and stature. Perhaps causing them to be not as athletic in comparison to the slightly smaller competitors in the Super Heavy etc… weight classes, that contain a weight class.











There seems to be no meaningful difference between the GI and NO-GI categories and our overall trend holds.











Interestingly we do see a difference between Male and Female categories. With the Female category having a noticeably flatter distribution. This could imply that weight is less important to placing in the absolute for women. However our dataset is small enough that this may be caused by a small sample size. If we took data across all belt levels, or a larger set of tournaments we could be more confident in this trend.
